content: The study investigated the safety and adherence of an intermittent pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) regimen among Kenyan men who have sex with men (MSM) and female sex workers (FSW). Participants were randomized into four groups: daily oral FTC/TDF, daily placebo, intermittent oral FTC/TDF, or intermittent placebo. The intermittent regimen involved taking doses on Mondays, Fridays, and within two hours after sexual activity, with a maximum of one dose per day. The randomization ratio was 2:1:2:1, and participants were followed monthly for four months. Adherence to the medication was monitored using the Medication Event Monitoring System (MEMS). Sexual activity data were collected through daily text message (SMS) queries and timeline follow-back interviews with a one-month recall period. A total of 67 men and 5 women were enrolled in the study. Safety outcomes were comparable across all groups. Adherence to post-coital doses was low, with a median adherence rate of 26% (interquartile range: 14–50%). The response rates to SMS queries were also low, potentially affecting the accuracy of post-coital dosing adherence measurements. Despite this, the acceptability of PrEP was high across all dosing regimens. The study concluded that adherence to intermittent dosing regimens, particularly coitally-dependent doses, may be more challenging than adherence to daily dosing. However, intermittent dosing could still be a viable option for PrEP if intracellular drug levels sufficient to prevent HIV acquisition can be achieved with less-than-daily dosing and if barriers to adherence are addressed. Further research is needed to gather additional drug level data, qualitative insights into adherence barriers, and improved methods for measuring sexual activity. This will help determine whether adherence to post-coital PrEP can be comparable to standard regimens.
